newsitem.title: USA: GM CFO sees 1997 gains in North America.
newsitem.headline: GM CFO sees 1997 gains in North America.

text.p: General Motors Corp chief financial officer J. Michael Losh said 1997 will be a year of continuing improvement for GM's North American market share and profitability.
In a conference call, Losh told reporters that North American gains will offset a continued tough competitive situation for the automaker in Europe this year.

"As we look forward to '97, GM will get the bulk of its improvements here in North America, and we do expect to improve year to year," Losh said. "You'll see improvements in both profitability and market share in North America."

He said the improvement will be due chiefly to new vehicles the automaker is introducing in the North American market. He would not reval GM's market share targets but forecast gains in both the car and truck markets.
GM's combined U.S. car and truck market share dipped to about 31 percent in 1996 from 32.4 percent in 1995.
Losh said the new vehicles have a lower production cost, which will help improve their profitability.
GM also is expanding truck capacity by converting its Arlington, Texas, plant to sport/utility vehicle production later this year.
The profitability of GM's North American Operations, including the Delphi Automotive Systems parts unit, was ravaged by strikes in 1996, falling to $1.25 billion from $2.4 billion in 1995.
In the 1996 fourth quarter, the North American Operations posted a loss of $124 million, versus a year-earlier profit of $603 million.
Losh said the new products for 1997 will help GM cut its first quarter North American incentives slightly below the $739 per vehicle it spent in the 1996 fourth quarter.
However, GM will continue to respond to competitors' incentive actions, he said.
In Europe, Losh said, incentive costs for the 1997 first quarter will be slightly higher than a year ago because of the brutally competitive sales environment there.
GM's European automotive operations earned $99 million in the 1996 fourth quarter, down from $248 million a year earlier. European incentive costs soared to $580 per vehicle from $326 a year earlier.
Losh said he expects GM's 1996 fourth quarter results in Europe will turn out to be the strongest of its major European rivals, but relief from market improvement is not expected soon.
"Europe will continue to be tough in 1997," he said.
The remainder of GM's International Operations, including Latin America and Asia/Pacific, earned $254 million in the 1996 fourth quarter versus $250 million a year earlier.
Losh said the current weakness of the yen against the dollar is giving Japanese automakers a price advantage that is hurting GM, Ford Motor Co and Chrysler Corp.
He said the current exchange rate of about 121.3 yen to the dollar is "not sustainable."
